# Introduction

<!-- Related work: closest-paper positioning. Characterizations are from titles
     and venues; confirm against the papers before submission. Fold into the
     intro contribution list once the intro is drafted. -->

Our analysis is most closely related to \citet{coughlin2026}, who estimates a
model of Medicare Part D plan choice under limited consideration in which
non-monetary plan attributes play a central role. We share the premise that
observed plan choices reflect limited consideration rather than full-information
preference, so that enrollment in dominated plans need not imply that
beneficiaries prefer them. Our analysis remains distinct in three ways. First,
we study Medicare Advantage rather than the stand-alone Part D drug benefit, so
the choice is over bundled medical coverage against an outside option of
traditional Medicare. Second, we identify consideration from observed search
behavior, using the search indicators in the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey
together with Plan Finder cost-rank and broker-channel prominence, rather than
inferring the consideration set from choice data alone. Third, our counterfactual
evaluates a decision-support intervention that lowers search costs, decomposing
the welfare change into a plan-value channel and a search-cost channel.

Our strategy for separating consideration from preference builds on
\citet{barseghyan2021}, who show how heterogeneity in consumers' choice sets can
be disentangled from heterogeneity in their preferences when the choice set is
only partially observed.

# Empirical Strategy

<!-- Draft of the structural core. Equations from
     code/analysis/vrdc/3-individual-likelihood.R; estimates in Table 1 are
     preliminary and hand-transcribed, to be rebuilt from standard_errors.csv. -->

We estimate a demand-side model of Medicare Advantage plan choice under limited
consideration. The model has three stages, consideration, search, and choice,
and is fit by joint maximum likelihood over the observed search actions and the
realized plan choice. The point of the three-stage structure is that a plan can
go unchosen for reasons choice data alone cannot separate, namely that it was
never considered, that considering it was too costly, or that it was considered
and preferred less. Limited consideration lets the model attribute part of the
observed enrollment in dominated plans to consideration rather than preference.

In the choice stage, a beneficiary who considers plan $j$ receives utility

\begin{equation}
v_{ij} = -\alpha_{\text{prem}} \frac{p_{ij}}{1000} - \alpha_{\text{oop}} \frac{o_{ij}}{1000}
  + \mathbf{1}[j=\text{FFS}]\,\xi_{\text{FFS}}
  + \mathbf{1}[j\in\text{MA}]\bigl(\beta (Q_j - 3.5) + \rho\, D_j + \text{cat}_j\bigr)
  + \psi\, \mathbf{1}[j=\text{inc}_i] + \varepsilon_{ij},
\label{eq:utility}
\end{equation}

where $p_{ij}$ is the premium and $o_{ij}$ the beneficiary-specific expected
out-of-pocket cost, both in thousands of dollars, $Q_j$ is the plan's star
rating, $D_j$ indicates Part D coverage, $\text{cat}_j$ is a plan-category effect
for PPO and PFFS relative to the omitted HMO category, $\xi_{\text{FFS}}$ is the
traditional-Medicare intercept, and $\psi$ is an incumbent-plan term that
captures state dependence \citep{handel2013}. Premium and expected out-of-pocket
cost enter separately rather than as a single cost, following \citet{abaluck2011},
so the model does not impose that a dollar of premium and a dollar of expected
out-of-pocket cost weigh equally. The specification carries no cost-variance term,
following the Medicare Advantage demand model of \citet{curto2021}, which likewise
includes no risk term in utility. With $\varepsilon_{ij}$
Type-I extreme value, the probability that $i$ chooses $j$ marginalizes over the
unobserved consideration set, following the consideration-set logit of
\citet{goeree2008}, as $P_{ij} = \phi_{ij} e^{v_{ij}} / \sum_k \phi_{ik} e^{v_{ik}}$, where $\phi_{ij}$
is the probability that $j$ enters $i$'s consideration set.

Traditional Medicare and the incumbent plan are considered with certainty
($\phi = 1$). For every other MA plan, the inclusion probability rises with the
beneficiary's consideration breadth $K_i = \exp(b_0 + b_{\text{info}} a_i^{\text{info}}
+ b_{\text{web}} a_i^{\text{web}} + b_{\text{phone}} a_i^{\text{phone}} + b_{\text{book}} a_i^{\text{book}})$,
built from the observed search actions $a_i$, and with the plan's market-level
prominence $\eta_j = \lambda_{\text{PF}} s_j^{\text{PF}} + \lambda_{\text{broker}} s_j^{\text{broker}}$,
where $s_j^{\text{PF}}$ is the plan's Plan Finder cost-rank score and
$s_j^{\text{broker}}$ its broker-channel prominence.

Search is a costly choice that broadens consideration. The per-beneficiary
search cost is

$$
c_i = \exp\bigl(\gamma' X_i + \sigma_\alpha \nu_i\bigr),
$$

where $X_i$ collects demeaned demographics (log income, education, age, dual
status, area deprivation), handbook comprehension, Medicare tenure, and two
self-reports of how costly comparing plans is, and $\nu_i$ is a standard normal
drawn once per beneficiary, so $\sigma_\alpha$ is the scale of a persistent
person-level search-cost component identified from the panel. Each of five search
indicators (sought information, visited medicare.gov, called 1-800-Medicare, read
the handbook, and reviews options, the last two ordered) fires through a logit in
the index $B_i - c_i - \kappa_a$, where $\kappa_a$ is an indicator-specific
threshold and $B_i$ is the benefit of considering the full menu over the
no-search default of traditional Medicare plus the incumbent, measured as the
difference in inclusive values. Because $B_i$ is built from the beneficiary's own
expected costs against the local county menu, it varies across counties for a
fixed person, which is what separates the benefit of search from its cost.

We estimate the 33 parameters by simulated maximum likelihood, integrating the
action likelihood over 50 common random draws of $\nu_i$ per beneficiary and
weighting by the survey weights. The objective is optimized with a derivative-free
subplex routine, since the simulated likelihood is not smooth in the consideration
thresholds. Standard errors are the sandwich $H^{-1} J H^{-1}$, with $J$ the outer
product of the per-beneficiary scores and $H$ the observed-information Hessian.

We find that beneficiaries respond to premiums far more strongly than to expected
out-of-pocket cost. The premium disutility is $\alpha_{\text{prem}} = 0.770$ (se
0.054) and the expected-out-of-pocket disutility is $\alpha_{\text{oop}} = 0.095$
(se 0.033), both positive and significant. A dollar of premium therefore reduces
utility about eight times as much as a dollar of expected out-of-pocket cost, the
premium-overweighting pattern documented by \citet{abaluck2011}. The expected
out-of-pocket coefficient is small but significantly different from zero, so the
overweighting is a matter of degree rather than beneficiaries ignoring
out-of-pocket cost entirely. Quality enters positively, with a star-rating
coefficient of $\beta = 0.449$ (se 0.052); at the estimated premium weight a
one-star improvement is worth about \$580 in annual premium. Part D coverage
carries a large positive coefficient ($\rho = 1.327$), and the incumbent term
$\psi = 4.662$ (se 0.082) is large and precisely estimated, reproducing the high
year-over-year retention in the data. Relative to HMO plans, PFFS plans are
valued less ($-0.467$, se 0.123) while PPO plans are statistically
indistinguishable.

The search-cost gradient has the expected signs on the dimensions where
interpretation is clear. Education and income both lower the search cost
($\gamma_{\text{educ}} = -0.058$, se 0.004; $\gamma_{\text{inc}} = -0.052$, se
0.022), while age and dual-eligibility raise it ($\gamma_{\text{age}} = 0.015$,
se 0.002; $\gamma_{\text{dual}} = 0.136$, se 0.044). Handbook comprehension and
the two self-reports of how costly comparing plans is each enter significantly,
which gives the cost level a direct measurement rather than leaving it to be
backed out of the search-benefit index alone. The random-effect scale is
significant ($\log \sigma_\alpha = 0.104$, se 0.027), so the panel identifies a
persistent person-level component of the search cost beyond what the observables
explain.

The consideration block is estimated less sharply. The breadth intercept $b_0 =
2.555$ (se 0.117) is precise, but the action-specific breadth loadings are
imprecise, and the two prominence weights are weakly identified, with the Plan
Finder weight significant only at the ten-percent level ($\lambda_{\text{PF}} =
0.517$, se 0.269) and the broker weight indistinguishable from zero
($\lambda_{\text{broker}} = 1.411$, se 1.125). The conditional-independence
assumption underlying the five-indicator measurement is examined separately in
the robustness analysis.

These estimates are preliminary. The likelihood was optimized to the evaluation
cap rather than to a convergence tolerance, and a warm restart to confirm the
solution is pending, so the point estimates and the sample size in
Table~\ref{tab:estimates} may change before the final version.
